results.summary: This project implements an 8-bit RISC-V-inspired CPU with a hardware multiplier, 32 bytes of RAM, and custom branching instructions. It uses a multi-cycle finite state machine for fetch, decode, and execute, and includes a bootloader mode for loading programs via the input pins. The CPU outputs the destination register value and program counter for debugging, and requires only a clock source and optional logic analyzer or LEDs for testing. Notable features include its high-density synthesis on the IHP26a process and the ability to step through programs manually at low clock speeds.

DUMB-Turing is a hardware implementation of a Turing machine based on Turing's original mathematical construction, using external SPI ROM and RAM for the transition table and tape. It supports 128 states and an alphabet size of 256, and requires one 512Kbit ROM and one 512Kbit RAM for operation. Testing is difficult because the memory devices must be pre-filled with data, and the author plans to provide updated instructions for building the transition table. The design is notable for its literal interpretation of a Turing machine and its reliance on external memory.

This design implements a custom SPI bridge to interface with RHD2164 neural amplifier chips, selecting specific channels and transferring data to an MCU via SPI. It also includes a register bank accessible via SPI or scan chain/shift register. Testing can be done by connecting to an FPGA with emulators or to an actual RHD2164 chip in CMOS or LVDS mode, with the selected data going to an MCU. The design is notable for its application in neural signal processing and its flexible register access.

Spacewar is a scaled-down graphics prototype of the classic Spacewar game, adhering to demoscene specifications for VGA and audio. It uses a SNES controller PMOD for input and outputs VGA signals for display. Testing is planned with CocoTB, but no test infrastructure is currently provided. The design requires external VGA and SNES PMODs to operate.

Underflow Cubed is a four-tile demo for the TTSKY26a demo competition, featuring 3D scenes rendered with a custom per-scanline ray tracing algorithm and a 24-voice synthesizer with delta-sigma modulated PWM audio output. It includes a sequencer that generates melodies, chords, and bass patterns based on a selectable key and scale. The design requires a TinyVGA Pmod and Mike's audio Pmod for output, and starts automatically after reset. Notable features include the speedup option to skip unused cycles, which trades off PWM resolution and rendering quality for higher clock speeds.

This project implements a 12-hour clock displayed with triangles rendered by a race-the-beam triangle rasterizer, using a state machine to incrementally draw three triangles based on edge equations while generating VGA timing. The second, minute, and hour hands are updated every frame by indexing into tables of edge equations. It requires a TinyVGA Pmod connected to a VGA monitor, and input pins allow advancing the minute and hour hands. Silicon testing confirmed it works as a clock and the time can be adjusted.

This design is a systolic binary neural network accelerator with 16 neurons, using an XNOR dot product engine, hardware feature expansion, signed bias, and a balanced popcount tree. It processes one bit per clock cycle over 8 cycles, reusing hardware to reduce silicon area compared to a fully parallel design. No external hardware is required, but a Raspberry Pi or Arduino can load trained weights and run inference via the input pins. The design is notable for its efficient systolic implementation and detailed documentation including version history.

Cgates tests two different implementations of Muller's C-gate—one built from a latch and one from combinatorial logic—and uses them to build 4, 16, and 64-stage rings. The C-gate outputs hold state unless both inputs agree, and the rings toggle a flip-flop each time a pulse circulates, allowing measurement of stage delay. Testing requires setting the two inputs and observing the outputs, with an oscilloscope needed for the faster rings. Silicon results show both C-gate implementations work, and the longest rings toggle slowly enough to be observed, though one tester noted a sick waveform on one output.

This project is a placeholder with the title 'idk yet' and minimal documentation, described only as 'It works' with no further explanation. It has input pins labeled 'ttin' and output pins labeled 'ttout', but no functional description or test instructions are provided. No external hardware is mentioned, and the design appears to be a template or experiment in Wokwi. Due to the lack of documentation, its purpose and capabilities cannot be determined.

This design implements a 32-bit iterative multiply-accumulate unit for tiny ML accelerators, using a 7x8-bit multiplier to produce a 15-bit product each clock cycle. A controller FSM shifts partial sums and aligns bias bytes across four training phases or one inference phase. It is tested with Cocotb against a Python reference model, covering training cycles, early-exit paths, and inference lockstep. No external hardware is required beyond the Tiny Tapeout carrier, though a host MCU can stream weights and bias bytes via GPIO.
